title: The person the size of a thumb
theme: After the offerings to the breaths, the eater turns from the food to the one who abides within: the thumb-sized person, lord of the whole world, who is satisfied by the meal.

words.meaning: of the measure of a thumb
words.context: the anonymous commentator: «स्वाङ्गुष्ठपरिमितः» — the size of one’s own thumb

words.role: joins the two qualifiers of puruṣaḥ
words.context: the anonymous commentator takes it to add the head as well: «चकारान्मस्तकं चाऽऽश्रितः»
the anonymous commentator: «ईशो नियन्ता» — the controller
the anonymous commentator reads it as a wish: «अनेन भोजनेन प्रीतो भवतु» — may he be pleased by this meal
the anonymous commentator: «सर्व जगद्भुङ्क्ते» — he consumes the whole world

sandhi.rule: puruṣaḥ + aṅguṣṭham → puruṣo ’ṅguṣṭham: -aḥ becomes -o and the following a is elided, marked by the avagraha.
The Taittirīya recitation writes a visarga before a sibilant as the sibilant doubled: īśaḥ sarvasya → īśas sarvasya.

samasa.meaning: the one who eats, enjoys, the whole

morphology.note: aṅguṣṭha with -mātra, ‘having the measure of’: a word of size, not a compound of two independent words.
Present indicative of √prī (9th class): ‘is pleased’. The Tirupati e-text and the text printed with Sāyaṇa read the imperative प्रीणातु, ‘may he be pleased’ (see flags).
Nominative of the root-noun -bhuj, ‘eating, enjoying’: the final j becomes k in the pausal form.

translation.literal: The person of a thumb’s measure, and resting on the thumb, the lord of the whole world, the master, the eater of all, is pleased.
translation.readable: The Person the size of a thumb, who rests in the thumb — lord of the whole world, its master, who partakes of all — is satisfied.

anvaya: अङ्गुष्ठमात्रः अङ्गुष्ठम् च समाश्रितः पुरुषः सर्वस्य जगतः ईशः प्रभुः विश्वभुक् प्रीणाति
syntax: One sentence. The subject puruṣaḥ carries two qualifiers joined by ca (aṅguṣṭhamātraḥ, aṅguṣṭhaṃ samāśritaḥ); three nouns stand in apposition to it (īśaḥ … prabhuḥ … viśvabhuk), the first two governing the genitive sarvasya jagataḥ; the verb prīṇāti comes last but one.

ambiguities.note: The base reads the indicative (‘is pleased’); the Tirupati e-text and the text printed with Sāyaṇa read the imperative (‘may he be pleased’). The anonymous commentator, on the base, still glosses a wish («प्रीतो भवतु»), and Bhāskara glosses both forms («प्रीणाति विश्वभुक्», «प्रीणातु तृप्यतु»).

The anonymous commentator and Sāyaṇa: the individual self, limited by the intellect in the thumb-sized space of the heart, which in its own nature is the lord of the world. Bhāskara: the Lord himself, called thumb-sized because he is perceived in the heart, which has that measure.

For the anonymous commentator the person rests on the thumb and, by ca, on the head as well: it pervades the body from foot to head. Bhāskara ties the words to the rite: with this verse water from the hand is let flow over the right thumb.

metre.name: anuṣṭubh
metre.note: Bhāskara names it an anuṣṭubh («अङ्गुष्ठेत्यनुष्टुभा»). As printed the two half-verses count 15 and 16 syllables: puruṣo ’ṅguṣṭham elides one a; read with the a, the first half also has 16.

beginner: This short verse belongs to the prayers said at a meal. After the first mouthfuls have been offered to the breaths within the body, the eater turns to the one who is said to dwell within: a ‘person the size of a thumb’. The old commentators explain the size: the space in the heart is about as big as a thumb, so the one who lives there is described by that measure. The verse then says this same inner person is the lord and master of the whole world and the one who ‘eats’ everything, and that he is satisfied. The anonymous commentator reads it as a wish that the Lord be pleased by the meal. Bhāskara adds that at this point water is poured over the right thumb. The edition reports the rite as the commentators describe it and makes no claim about its effects.
analogy: Like a small window through which the whole sky is seen: the small measure belongs to the opening, not to what is seen through it.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: A person of a thumb’s measure, resting on the thumb, is called the lord of the whole world, its master and the eater of all, and is said to be pleased.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator places it after the meal’s first offerings, once the restlessness hunger causes has settled: «क्षुदादिजनितचित्तविक्षेपशान्तेरूर्ध्वं भोक्तुर्जीवस्य परमेश्वरस्वरूपानुसंधानहेतुं मन्त्रं दर्शयति» — a mantra by which the one who eats calls to mind the nature of the supreme Lord. Sāyaṇa says the same in nearly the same words («भोक्तुर्जीवस्य परमेश्वररूपत्वानुसंधाने हेतुभूतं मन्त्रं दर्शयति»). Bhāskara gives the act that goes with it: «दक्षिणाङ्गुष्ठे पाणिजलं स्रावपति» — one lets water from the hand flow over the right thumb.

commentary.label: comparative
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator measures it by the heart: «हृदयमध्यगत आकाशः स्वाङ्गुष्ठपरिमितः» — the space in the middle of the heart is the size of one’s thumb; the intellect there has that size, and the individual self limited by it is called thumb-sized («जीवरूपः पुरुषोऽप्यङ्गुष्ठमात्रः»). Without that limiting adjunct, in its true form, it is the controller of the world («स चोपाधिसंबन्धमन्तरेण स्वकीयेन वास्तवरूपेण सर्वस्य जगत ईशो नियन्ता»). Bhāskara starts from the Lord: unlimited, he is called thumb-sized because he is found in the heart, which has that measure («ईश्वरो ऽनवच्छिन्नोप्य् अङ्गुष्ठप्रमाणहृदयदेशोपलम्भात्»).

commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: The base has the indicative prīṇāti, ‘is pleased’. The Tirupati e-text and the text Sāyaṇa comments on read the imperative prīṇātu, and Sāyaṇa glosses it «प्रीणातु, अनेन भोजनेन प्रीतो भवतु». The anonymous commentator, commenting on prīṇāti, also gives the sense of a wish. Bhāskara explains prīṇāti first and then glosses «प्रीणातु तृप्यतु», ‘may he be pleased, satisfied’.

schools.disagreement: No Vedānta-school commentary on this text is in the edition’s sources: Raṅgarāmānuja’s is not available, and the commentaries present (the anonymous bhāṣya, Sāyaṇa, Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara) are ritual and Vedic explanations, not school readings. Between the commentators present, the anonymous commentator and Sāyaṇa read the thumb-sized person as the individual self whose true nature is the Lord; Bhāskara reads it as the Lord found in the heart.

parallels.note: The Kaṭha speaks of the same thumb-sized person standing in the middle of the self, lord of past and future.

parallels.quote: अङ्गुष्ठमात्रः पुरुषोऽन्तरात्मा सदा जनानां हृदये सन्निविष्टः
parallels.note: The Kaṭha places the thumb-sized person in the heart as the inner self, as the commentators here do.

contemporary.text: The verse comes at the point of a meal when hunger has eased, and turns attention from the food to the one who is fed. Pausing after the first relief of hunger to recognise what sustains one is a habit many traditions share. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: Why might a prayer at a meal speak of the one within rather than of the food?
reflect.deeper: The anonymous commentator says the thumb-size belongs to the space of the heart and not to the person in it. What does that distinction let him say about the person?
reflect.practice: At your next meal, pause once after the first few mouthfuls before going on.

references.text: Sāyaṇa’s comment on this verse is his anuvāka 38. In the edition’s Sāyaṇa file it is filed under 38 together with his comments on 10.70 and 10.74 (his anuvākas 36 and 37), which the source prints on the same pages.
Bhāskara’s comment is his anuvāka 38 (the Drāviḍa numbering).

flags.note: प्रीणाति (base and the Ānandāśrama pariśiṣṭa text) against प्रीणातु (the Tirupati e-text, and the text printed with Sāyaṇa): the collation leaves it for review; the edition keeps the base.
The Ānandāśrama pariśiṣṭa text prints प्रभु without the visarga; the base and the Tirupati e-text have प्रभुः.
The thumb-sized person as the individual self (the anonymous commentator, Sāyaṇa) or as the Lord (Bhāskara): the commentators differ, and the text does not decide.
The edition’s computed map gives no Sāyaṇa anuvāka for 10.71; his comment is in sayana:38 and is cited explicitly. The Bhāskara map (38) is right.
